sections.title: The Core Idea: Transplant Oncology and How Candidates Are Chosen
sections.markdown:
# Liver transplantation as a treatment for cancer

Liver transplantation was developed to replace a failing liver. Surgeons now also use it to remove cancer that sits in the liver and cannot be cut out any other way. This field is called **transplant oncology**, meaning the treatment of cancer through transplant medicine and surgery. The review collects the current evidence for each cancer that transplantation is used for, explains how centres decide who qualifies, and describes the techniques being developed to deal with a basic constraint: there are not enough donor livers.

Six cancers are covered:

- colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver
- two bile duct cancers (hilar and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma)
- neuroendocrine tumours that have spread to the liver
- hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common cancer that starts in the liver
- a rare vascular tumour called hepatic epithelioid haemangioendothelioma

After these, the review takes up two issues that apply to every cancer: how anti-rejection drugs affect the chance of the cancer returning, and how machine perfusion and other methods can enlarge the donor supply.

## The concepts behind the decisions

Four ideas from cancer surgery frame who gets a transplant.

Resectability asks whether the tumour can be removed with ordinary liver surgery. It is less objective than it sounds. Some procedures make the remaining liver grow before a large resection, such as portal vein embolization or ALPPS (a two-stage operation). Others are extreme, such as taking the liver out, operating on it outside the body and putting it back. Centres use all of these under their own rules, so a tumour called unresectable in one hospital may be operable in another.

Operability asks whether the patient's general health can withstand the surgery and anaesthesia. Curability depends on scale. For one patient, cure means the disease never returns (for example, no recurrence at 5 years). For a population, it can mean death rates falling back to those of the general public. Transplantability refers to national or institutional rules for joining the waiting list. These rules weigh the risk of dropping off the list through death or cancer progression, the risk of death after transplant, and how many organs are available.

Because donor livers are scarce, giving one to a cancer patient who might relapse raises ethical questions. The authors put one measure at the centre of these decisions. **Transplant benefit** is the extra survival a transplant gives compared with the best alternative:

transplant benefit = survival after liver transplant - survival with the best alternative treatment

The International Liver Transplantation Society (ILTS) consensus guidelines say this should be one of the main factors in setting selection criteria.

Living donor liver transplantation (LDLT), in which a healthy person gives part of their liver, comes up throughout the review. Patients do not have to wait for a deceased donor, and surgeons can time the operation to fit a chemotherapy schedule. The cost is that a healthy donor has to accept surgical risk.

sections.title: Colorectal Metastases and Bile Duct Cancers
sections.markdown:
## Colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver

About half of people with colorectal cancer develop metastases, and the liver is the most common site. Surgical removal is the only treatment that can cure these colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). Better chemotherapy and staged liver operations have made more of them removable. Even so, 75 to 80% of patients can only have palliative chemotherapy, and about 10% of them are alive at 5 years.

The SECA-I trial, published in 2013, was the first controlled proof-of-concept study of transplanting unresectable CRLM. Overall survival was 95% at 1 year, 68% at 3 years and 60% at 5 years. Disease-free survival was low, only 35% at 1 year. However, most recurrences were slow-growing lung metastases that surgeons could remove, so patients lived well despite relapsing.

The trial found four risk factors for worse survival, which became the **Oslo score**:

- largest tumour over 5.5 cm
- less than 2 years between surgery for the original bowel cancer and the transplant
- CEA, a blood tumour marker, above 80 μg/l
- cancer growing during chemotherapy at the time of transplant

Oslo score = number of these four factors present (0 to 4)

Ten-year results, published in 2022, showed that patients scoring 0 or 1 had 75% survival at 5 years and 50% at 10 years.

The follow-up trial, SECA-II, used stricter entry rules shaped by the Oslo factors. Survival at 1, 3 and 5 years was 100%, 83% and 83%. Disease-free survival was 53%, 44% and 35% at 1, 2 and 3 years. About 70% of recurrences were in the lung, and most could be removed. Among patients who relapsed, 73% were alive 4 years after the recurrence. The authors take this as evidence that disease-free survival is a poor measure of how well transplantation works for CRLM, because many patients relapse and still live for years.

The Oslo score alone is not enough to select patients. Worse outcomes also follow a primary tumour on the right side of the colon, a BRAF mutation, and undifferentiated or signet ring cell tumours. PET/CT scans are used to check for cancer outside the liver. A metabolic tumour volume below 70 cm3 on the pre-transplant scan strongly predicts good survival, and the authors recommend measuring it routinely.

The TransMet trial gave the strongest evidence. It randomly assigned patients with unresectable CRLM to either transplant plus chemotherapy or chemotherapy alone. These patients had a heavy tumour burden, with a median of 20 metastases. After a median follow-up of 59.3 months, 5-year survival counting every patient in the group they were assigned to (intention-to-treat) was 56.6% with transplant and 12.6% with chemotherapy. Among patients who actually received their assigned treatment, the figures were 73.3% and 9.3%. That makes CRLM the only transplant oncology indication supported by level 1 evidence, the highest grade, which comes from randomized trials.

As more centres adopt the approach, donor supply becomes the limit. Living donation has been used mainly in Asia, with results similar to other published series. Split livers, where one deceased donor liver is divided between two recipients, can help, though allocation systems that rank patients by MELD score (a measure of liver disease severity) can limit the gain.

The RAPID procedure, introduced in 2015, takes a different approach. The surgeon removes the left side of the patient's liver and implants a small graft (segments 2 and 3, a small left portion of a donor liver) beside the remaining native liver. Blood flow from the portal vein is then redirected to the graft so that it grows quickly. Once it is large enough, usually after 2 to 3 weeks, a second operation removes the rest of the diseased liver. A study across seven European centres found the procedure safe, with good regrowth and the second operation done after a median of 2 weeks. RAPID works with split deceased-donor livers or with living donors. The living-donor version is attractive because the donor gives only a small piece, which lowers donor risk, while the recipient still gains a large benefit. CRLM patients usually have otherwise healthy livers without high portal pressure or liver failure, so they cope with smaller grafts better than transplant patients with chronic liver disease.

## Hilar cholangiocarcinoma

Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (hCCA) is bile duct cancer at the point where the ducts leave the liver. Thomas Starzl performed the first transplant for it in 1963, but early results were very poor. Of five patients who lived beyond 2 months, four relapsed and died. Transplantation for this cancer was nearly abandoned. The authors blame poor patient selection and the lack of strict chemotherapy protocols before surgery.

The Mayo Clinic changed this in 2000 with a protocol of chemoradiation (radiation combined with the drug 5-fluorouracil) before transplant. The first 11 patients had a median survival of 44 months and only one recurrence. A 2004 follow-up of 28 patients reported 82% survival at 5 years and a 14.2% recurrence rate.

**Selection.** Under the Mayo criteria, later adopted by the US organ-sharing network UNOS, the tumour must be unresectable and under 3 cm. The diagnosis has to be confirmed by brush cytology, and/or the patient must have a malignant-looking narrowing of the bile duct with the tumour marker CA19-9 above 100 U/ml. The patient must not have had a previous surgical exploration or a biopsy through the skin or abdominal cavity. Diagnosis is hard because brushings often miss cancer. Adding FISH, a genetic test for abnormal chromosome numbers, improves accuracy. Spread to lymph nodes or any other site rules out transplant absolutely, so nodes are biopsied with endoscopic ultrasound before chemoradiation starts.

sections.title: Neuroendocrine Tumours, Hepatocellular Carcinoma and a Rare Vascular Tumour
sections.markdown:
## Neuroendocrine tumours

Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) account for only about 0.5% of cancers, but most patients develop liver metastases, often in both lobes. Treatment combines hormone-blocking drugs, surgery, ablation, systemic therapy and targeted radiation. When the metastases are too widespread to debulk, transplantation has been proposed as a cure.

Because the disease is rare and slow, no high-quality comparisons of treatments exist, and the evidence comes from registries and single centres. European registry data show 5-year survival of 47 to 70% and recurrence of 31 to 57%. Survival rose from 46% for patients transplanted before 2000 to 59% after, which the authors attribute to better selection. Poor prognostic signs include cancer outside the liver, removing the primary tumour during the transplant operation, and vascular or lymph node involvement.

In 2016 the Milan group reported 5- and 10-year survival of 97% and 89%, and their criteria became the standard in most programmes:

- low-grade tumour (Ki67 below 10%)
- a primary tumour draining into the portal venous system, fully removed before transplant
- no more than 50% of the liver involved
- responsive or stable disease for at least 6 months
- age 55 or younger (later raised to 60)

The Milan group estimated the transplant benefit at 6.82 months by 5 years and 38.43 months by 10 years. A 2021 comparison of patients within the Milan criteria found 5- and 10-year survival of 95% and 93% after transplant against 90% and 75% after resection. Disease-free survival was 75% and 52% against 33% and 18%. A propensity-matched study, which pairs similar patients across the two treatments, found 10-year survival of 88.8% after transplant against 22.4% after resection, with disease progression in 13.1% against 89%.

Current European guidelines (ENETS) call transplant an option for highly selected, preferably young patients with hormone-related symptoms who stop responding early to medical treatment. The authors expect lutetium-177 radionuclide therapy to become both a competitor and a pre-transplant treatment, and they call for a prospective trial.

## Hepatocellular carcinoma

About 90% of hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC) arise in a damaged or cirrhotic liver, caused by hepatitis B or C, alcohol, fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems (MASLD) or other conditions. HCC differs from the other cancers here because the diseased liver itself is what produces tumours. It also tends to arise in several places at once: 50 to 60% of livers removed at transplant contain multiple tumours, and at least 30% of these were missed on scans. A transplant removes the tumours along with the liver that produced them. For HCC confined to the liver without invasion of major vessels, it gives the best long-term results.

**Early HCC.** The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system has guided staging and treatment for three decades. For a single tumour of 2 cm or less, ablation (destroying the tumour with heat) gives results similar to resection or transplant. For early-stage disease (one tumour, or up to three tumours of 3 cm or less), resection or ablation can be offered to patients without significant portal hypertension or who cannot have a transplant, but transplantation gives the best chance of cure. One strategy is to resect first and keep transplant as a backup if the cancer returns ("salvage" transplant). It performs poorly, because only 33% of patients who relapse end up getting a curative transplant. For a single tumour up to 3 cm, resection matches transplant and beats ablation. For multiple tumours or tumours of 3 to 5 cm, transplant is probably best.

**Intermediate HCC (BCLC stage B).** This is where the authors see the hardest problem. Most patients arrive with large or multiple tumours, and the MASLD epidemic is adding more late, aggressive cases. Before 2022 these patients received only non-curative systemic therapy. The classic transplant criteria (Milan and UCSF) count tumours and measure their size, and they turned out to be too restrictive. Well-selected patients beyond these limits had similar survival after transplant. Large expanded-criteria series (31 to 1556 patients) reported acceptable long-term survival with tumours up to 7.5 cm and up to three in number. Much of this push came from Asian centres, where deceased donors are scarce and patients who wait too long lose their chance.

Selection is shifting from size and count to tumour biology. Markers include the blood proteins AFP and PIVKA-II (both their level and how they change), response to downstaging treatment, how strongly the tumour shows up on FDG or FAPI PET scans, waiting time as a "test of time", inflammation ratios such as neutrophil-to-lymphocyte, and sometimes how the tumour looks under the microscope. Downstaging with TACE (chemotherapy delivered through the liver artery), TARE (radioactive beads delivered the same way) or focused radiotherapy works as a filter: tumours that shrink and whose markers fall are likely to behave well after transplant.

This work led to the 2022 BCLC update, which for the first time recommends transplant for selected stage B patients using extended criteria that combine tumour size and AFP. The update also introduced treatment stage migration, which lets doctors move a patient to the next treatment option when the first-line option is not feasible. Vitale and colleagues showed that transplant gives the largest survival benefit in patients with advanced cirrhosis and stage B or C disease without spread outside the liver, because these patients have no good alternatives. Going beyond the classic criteria costs 10 to 15% in long-term survival, but outcomes remain much better than with ablation or systemic therapy alone. In the authors' own study, the 5-year transplant benefit over TACE or TARE was 42 months for patients at low risk of recurrence and 25 months even for those at high risk.

sections.title: Issues Shared by Every Cancer: Anti-Rejection Drugs and Donor Shortage
sections.markdown:
## Do anti-rejection drugs fuel cancer recurrence?

Transplant patients take immunosuppressants for life. A weakened immune system can let cancer grow, and transplant recipients have higher rates of skin cancer, lymphoproliferative disorders and some other cancers. The effect differs by drug class, and HCC is where it has been studied most.

**Calcineurin inhibitors** (cyclosporin and tacrolimus) have long been the mainstay. They raise levels of TGF-β and VEGF, two signals that promote HCC. High exposure (cyclosporin blood trough above 300 ng/ml, tacrolimus above 10 ng/ml) is an independent risk factor for recurrence. Taking a calcineurin inhibitor alone carried more risk than a combined regimen with an antimetabolite and steroids. For cyclosporin, high cumulative doses in months 4 to 12 after transplant were most harmful. For tacrolimus, the effect was seen only in the first month, for reasons still unclear.

**mTOR inhibitors** (sirolimus and everolimus) work differently. They block a growth pathway (PI3K/Akt/mTOR) and reduce VEGF, which has anti-tumour effects. Studies comparing them with calcineurin inhibitors found better survival and less HCC recurrence, and the effect appears to hold across the drug class. Adding sirolimus to a calcineurin inhibitor improved recurrence-free survival up to 5 years. In a large registry, sirolimus helped HCC patients more than other transplant patients. The only randomized trial found benefit up to 5 years, mostly in patients at low risk of recurrence, with the best results on sirolimus alone. Steroids, azathioprine, IL-2 receptor antibodies and anti-thymocyte globulin have not been linked to recurrence.

Most of this evidence is retrospective, and the one randomized trial had few patients on sirolimus alone, so the authors stop short of firm recommendations and call for prospective trials.

## Organ shortage and marginal grafts

Some centres report that up to 20% of patients die while waiting for a liver. Donors are getting older and more often have diabetes or obesity, which lowers graft quality. Expanding transplant to cancer patients adds to the demand.

One response is to use livers from donors after cardiac death (DCD) and "marginal" livers from donors after brain death (DBD). DCD livers carry higher risks of injury when blood flow returns, grafts that never work, and bile duct narrowing. The ILTS describes an "ideal" donor as aged 60 or younger, with a BMI of 30 or less, under 30% fat in the liver, and less than 8 hours of cold storage. It recommends no more than 30 minutes of functional warm ischaemia, counted from the point when the dying donor's oxygen saturation falls below 80% or blood pressure falls below 60 mmHg until the organ is flushed with cold solution. Centres have stretched these limits, including successful use of DCD donors over 70. Up to 50% of marginal DBD livers are declined.

Machine perfusion is changing what counts as usable. Normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) keeps the liver at body temperature with circulating fluid so doctors can test whether it works before transplanting it. In the VITTAL trial, NMP testing allowed 71% of previously discarded livers perfused with the intent to transplant to be used, with 100% patient and graft survival at 90 days. Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) pumps oxygenated fluid through the liver at 4 to 10°C, which lowers its metabolism while repairing cells and clearing waste. A dual version (D-HOPE), perfusing through both the hepatic artery and portal vein, was tested in a European randomized trial of DCD livers. It cut non-anastomotic bile duct strictures by 64%, post-reperfusion syndrome by 57% and early graft dysfunction by 39%. Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) restores circulation inside the donor before the organs are removed, and retrospective studies show fewer complications than with marginal DCD livers and results comparable to standard DBD livers.

For cancer patients, perfusion has two further advantages. Early data suggest HOPE may reduce HCC recurrence. Perfusion also lets centres schedule transplants in the daytime, which helps when frozen-section pathology is needed during surgery.

sections.title: Follow-Up After Transplant and What Comes Next
sections.markdown:
## Follow-up after transplant

Follow-up aims to catch recurrence early, especially when there are only a few metastases that targeted treatment can still reach. One experienced centre treated HCC recurrences after living-donor transplant with combined therapies and reported survival of 57% at 1 year and 24% at 3 years, with one patient living 7.5 years after recurrence. A sample HCC protocol uses a CT scan every 6 months for 2 years and then yearly (PET-CT if the tumour originally showed up on PET), abdominal ultrasound every 3 months for 2 years and then every 6 months, and AFP and/or PIVKA-II blood tests on the same schedule as the ultrasound. Where resources are limited, closer follow-up can be kept for patients at higher risk or those transplanted beyond the classic criteria. Risk scores used in HCC, such as SIMAP500 and RECIST-based scoring, could be adapted for other cancers.

The authors expect cancer to remain a lasting reason for liver transplantation. They predict that selection criteria will keep changing as tumour biology is measured more precisely with radiomics (quantitative image analysis), cancer genomics and tests for tumour DNA and RNA circulating in the blood. Except in colorectal metastases, randomized evidence is missing and patient numbers are small, and they propose international prospective registries to fill that gap.

anchors.sentence: Studies comparing them with calcineurin inhibitors found better survival and less HCC recurrence, and the effect appears to hold across the drug class.
anchors.quote: It appears to be a potential class effect as similar significant differences in HCC recurrence and survival have been observed with everolimus compared with CNIs.

anchors.sentence: Adding sirolimus to a calcineurin inhibitor improved recurrence-free survival up to 5 years.
anchors.quote: Furthermore, the combined sirolimus/CNI regimen had significantly improved recurrence-free survival up to 5 years compared with the CNI-only regimen, suggesting potential antagonism of the known procarcinogenic effects of CNI in HCC recurrence and antitumour advantage.

anchors.sentence: In a large registry, sirolimus helped HCC patients more than other transplant patients.
anchors.quote: Interestingly, in a large retrospective registry-based cohort study, sirolimus survival benefit was greater in patients transplanted for HCC than patients without HCC, suggesting a specific benefit for the HCC cohort post-transplant.

anchors.sentence: The only randomized trial found benefit up to 5 years, mostly in patients at low risk of recurrence, with the best results on sirolimus alone.
anchors.quote: In the only randomized clinical trial, recurrence-free survival and OS were noted up to 5 years post-transplantation, particularly in those with low risk of HCC recurrence, and the greatest recurrence-free survival and OS was noted in those patients on sirolimus monotherapy compared with combined immunosuppression regimens.

anchors.sentence: Steroids, azathioprine, IL-2 receptor antibodies and anti-thymocyte globulin have not been linked to recurrence.
anchors.quote: Further agents used for immunosuppression in liver transplantation, both for induction, acute rejection and maintenance, including corticosteroids, antimetabolites (for example azathioprine), anti-interleukin-2 receptor antibodies (ILR2a) and anti-thymoglobulin (ATG), have not been associated with HCC recurrence,,.

anchors.sentence: Most of this evidence is retrospective, and the one randomized trial had few patients on sirolimus alone, so the authors stop short of firm recommendations and call for prospective trials.
anchors.quote: However, most studies covering the impact of immunosuppression on HCC recurrence have been retrospective cohort studies, and a single randomized clinical trial had a relatively low number of patients on mTOR monotherapy, preventing firm recommendations.

anchors.sentence: Some centres report that up to 20% of patients die while waiting for a liver.
anchors.quote: Individual centres have reported waitlist mortality rates as high as 20%.

anchors.sentence: Donors are getting older and more often have diabetes or obesity, which lowers graft quality.
anchors.quote: While the organ donation rates remain variable, with an increasing ageing population and higher incidence of metabolic co-morbidities such as diabetes mellitus and obesity, reduced quality of the grafts is increasingly encountered.

anchors.sentence: Expanding transplant to cancer patients adds to the demand.
One response is to use livers from donors after cardiac death (DCD) and "marginal" livers from donors after brain death (DBD).
anchors.quote: Several attempts have been made to deal with the shortage and match the demand for the grafts, including the usage of donor after cardiac death (DCD) grafts and marginal donor after brain death (DBD) livers.

anchors.sentence: DCD livers carry higher risks of injury when blood flow returns, grafts that never work, and bile duct narrowing.
The ILTS describes an "ideal" donor as aged 60 or younger, with a BMI of 30 or less, under 30% fat in the liver, and less than 8 hours of cold storage.
anchors.quote: The causation is multifactorial based on which the ILTS consensus outlined criteria for ‘ideal’ donors, including donor age ≤60 years, donor BMI ≤30 kg/m2, macrovesicular steatosis <30% (in the absence of machine perfusion utilization) and cold ishemia time (CIT) <8 h.

anchors.sentence: It recommends no more than 30 minutes of functional warm ischaemia, counted from the point when the dying donor's oxygen saturation falls below 80% or blood pressure falls below 60 mmHg until the organ is flushed with cold solution.
anchors.quote: ILTS consensus guidelines recommend the definitions of total donor WIT as the withdrawal of treatment to cold flush, and functional donor (fDWIT) is the time point when either SpO2 is <80% or mean arterial pressure is <60 mmHg until cold flush.

anchors.sentence: Centres have stretched these limits, including successful use of DCD donors over 70.
anchors.quote: There have been successful reports of using DCD grafts from donors over 70 years,.

anchors.sentence: Up to 50% of marginal DBD livers are declined.
anchors.quote: Together with such risks and also due to ethical concerns, decline rates of livers as high as 50% have been reported.

anchors.sentence: Machine perfusion is changing what counts as usable.
Normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) keeps the liver at body temperature with circulating fluid so doctors can test whether it works before transplanting it.
anchors.quote: Functional assessment of a liver on normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) allows for evaluating the viability (Birmingham, Cambridge, Groningen criteria) and function before transplantation and will enable logistics.

anchors.sentence: In the VITTAL trial, NMP testing allowed 71% of previously discarded livers perfused with the intent to transplant to be used, with 100% patient and graft survival at 90 days.
anchors.quote: In this prospective, non-randomized, phase 2 trial, viability assessment with NMP allowed transplantation of 71% of discarded livers that were perfused with the intent of transplantation, with 100% 90-day patient and graft survival.

anchors.sentence: Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) pumps oxygenated fluid through the liver at 4 to 10°C, which lowers its metabolism while repairing cells and clearing waste.
anchors.quote: During HOPE, the liver is perfused at a temperature of 4–10°C with an oxygenated solution.

anchors.sentence: A dual version (D-HOPE), perfusing through both the hepatic artery and portal vein, was tested in a European randomized trial of DCD livers.
anchors.quote: Dual hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (D-HOPE) aims to optimize oxygen delivery to the liver cells (hepatocytes) and bile ducts (cholangiocytes), potentially reducing the risk of ischaemic injury more effectively than single vessel perfusion by perfusing the liver with oxygenated hypothermic saline both through the hepatic artery and portal vein.

anchors.sentence: It cut non-anastomotic bile duct strictures by 64%, post-reperfusion syndrome by 57% and early graft dysfunction by 39%.
anchors.quote: A European multicentre, randomized clinical trial on D-HOPE in regular DCD liver transplantation demonstrated a 64% reduction of non-anastomotic strictures (NAS), a 57% reduction in postreperfusion syndrome and a 39% reduction in early allograft dysfunction after transplantation.

anchors.sentence: Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) restores circulation inside the donor before the organs are removed, and retrospective studies show fewer complications than with marginal DCD livers and results comparable to standard DBD livers.
anchors.quote: Experience from retrospective studies has shown reduced early allograft dysfunction and the risk of primary non-function compared with marginal DCD grafts, fewer overall biliary complications, graft loss and death compared with marginal DCD livers.

anchors.sentence: For cancer patients, perfusion has two further advantages.
Early data suggest HOPE may reduce HCC recurrence.
anchors.quote: The influence of machine perfusion modalities on cancer recurrence is not fully understood, although early data suggests reduced recurrence rates in the HCC cohort using HOPE.

anchors.sentence: Perfusion also lets centres schedule transplants in the daytime, which helps when frozen-section pathology is needed during surgery.
anchors.quote: Some centres have started moving to make transplant surgery a daytime procedure by utilizing the perfusion modalities.

anchors.sentence: Follow-up aims to catch recurrence early, especially when there are only a few metastases that targeted treatment can still reach.
anchors.quote: Early reports have shown promising results with neoadjuvant treatment with sirolimus (mammalian target of rapamycin) before LT and some reports confirmed the role of systemic therapy for recurrence following LT using tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lenvatinib have also been described.

anchors.sentence: One experienced centre treated HCC recurrences after living-donor transplant with combined therapies and reported survival of 57% at 1 year and 24% at 3 years, with one patient living 7.5 years after recurrence.
anchors.quote: Experienced units have shown that with the use of multimodality treatment, 1-year and 3-year OS of 57 and 24% respectively, was achieved, with a maximum postrecurrence survival of 7.5 years among post-LDLT patients with HCC recurrence.

anchors.sentence: A sample HCC protocol uses a CT scan every 6 months for 2 years and then yearly (PET-CT if the tumour originally showed up on PET), abdominal ultrasound every 3 months for 2 years and then every 6 months, and AFP and/or PIVKA-II blood tests on the same schedule as the ultrasound.
anchors.quote: One such example of post-LT follow-up protocol for patients with HCC is a CT scan (PET-CT if the tumour was initially FDG-18 PET avid) 6 monthly for 2 years and then yearly, ultrasound of the abdomen every 3 monthly for 2 years and then 6 monthly, and serum AFP and/or PIVKA-II levels 3 monthly for 2 years and then 6 monthly.

anchors.sentence: Where resources are limited, closer follow-up can be kept for patients at higher risk or those transplanted beyond the classic criteria.
anchors.quote: In resource-constrained health systems, local protocols can be titred to those at higher risk of recurrence and for those beyond conventional criteria.

anchors.sentence: Risk scores used in HCC, such as SIMAP500 and RECIST-based scoring, could be adapted for other cancers.
anchors.quote: SIMAP500, RECIST scores risk stratify the need for follow-up among patients with HCC, and similar strategies can be applied in the wider transplant oncology programmes.

anchors.sentence: The authors expect cancer to remain a lasting reason for liver transplantation.

They predict that selection criteria will keep changing as tumour biology is measured more precisely with radiomics (quantitative image analysis), cancer genomics and tests for tumour DNA and RNA circulating in the blood.
anchors.quote: Conclusion: Cancer indications for liver transplantation are here to stay, and the selection criteria among all cancer groups are likely to evolve further with improved prognostication of tumour biology using adjuncts such as radiomics, cancer genomics, and circulating DNA and RNA status.

anchors.sentence: Except in colorectal metastases, randomized evidence is missing and patient numbers are small, and they propose international prospective registries to fill that gap.
anchors.quote: International prospective registry-based studies could overcome the limitations of smaller patient cohorts and lack of level 1 evidence.

sources.zraf034-s2.1/p5: A recent randomized clinical trial, TransMet, has compared liver transplantation + chemotherapy to chemotherapy alone in patients with unresectable CRLM. The study population had a high tumour load with a median of 20 metastases in both groups, and the delay from diagnosis to randomization was 15.9 months in the transplant arm. All transplanted patients but one had a low Oslo-score (<2). After a median follow-up of 59.3 months, the 5-year intention-to-treat survival in the LT cohort was 56.6% in the transplant group compared with 12.6% in the chemotherapy group. In per-protocol analysis, the corresponding 5-year survival rates were 73.3% and 9.3%. The outcomes of the TRANSMET trial confirm the principal findings from all the previous clinical trials on LT for CRLM and have the potential to change clinical practice since CRLM is the only transplant oncology indication that is supported by level 1 evidence.
sources.zraf034-s2.1/p2: The first controlled ‘proof of concept’ SEcondary CAncer (SECA-I) trial to explore LT in non-resectable CRLM was published in 2013 and found an estimated overall survival (OS) of 95%, 68% and 60% at 1, 3 and 5 years respectively. However, disease-free survival (DFS) was only 35% at 1 year. Still, most recurrences were slow-growing lung metastases that could be offered curative intent resection, thereby yielding a favourable overall survival despite recurrence post-transplant. Risk factors for inferior survival were maximal tumour diameter >5.5 cm, time from primary cancer surgery <2 years, CEA levels >80 μg/l and disease progression after chemotherapy at the time of LT. The four factors constitute the ‘Oslo-Score’ by assigning 1 point to each for risk stratification. The 10-year outcome data of the SECA-I trial was published in 2022 and showed that a low Oslo score of 0–1 is associated with a 5-year and 10-year actual OS of 75 and 50% respectively.

sources.zraf034-s2.4/p3: The Milan Group in 2016 published outstanding 5-year and 10-year OS of 97 and 89% respectively, with liver transplantation for NELM,. Milan NET-LT criteria are, therefore, generally accepted as a standard in most programmes. The group has reported an adjusted transplant-related survival benefit of 6.82 months (95% c.i. 1.10–12.54; P = 0.019) and 38.43 months (95% c.i. 21.41–55.45; P < 0.001) at 5 and 10 years respectively.
sources.zraf034-s2.6/p3: Meanwhile, Lai et al. established a prognostic scoring system by analysing the outcomes of 149 recipients undergoing LT for HEHE between 1984 and 2014 in the ELTR-ELITA registry. The 5-year post-LT OS and DFS rates were 79.5% and 79.4% respectively. The disease recurred in 37 (24.8%) patients after a median time of 18 months. Macrovascular invasion detected at pathology (HR 4.9; 95% c.i. 2.4–9.9), pre-LT waiting time ≤120 days (HR 2.5; 95% c.i. 1.2–5.3) and hilar lymph node invasion (HR 2.2; 95% c.i. 1.1–4.5) but not extrahepatic metastases, were found to be significant risk factors for post-LT recurrence. The HEHE-LT score was developed based on these three factors that successfully stratified the patients into three groups by their 5-year DFS rates: low score (0–2), 93.9% (n = 58), intermediate score (3–5), 76.9% (n = 74) and high score (6–10), 38.5% (n = 17). In 2020, the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) held a virtual consensus meeting involving >80 experts to reach a global consensus on HEHE management. This meeting concluded that LT for unresectable HEHE with no extrahepatic disease should be offered to patients ‘after full disclosure of the potential benefits and the risks’ associated with LT (level V evidence, Grade A recommendation).
sources.zraf034-s2.6.1/p3: Calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs), such as cyclosporin and tacrolimus, have long been used in immunosuppressive regimens post-transplantation. CNIs have been shown to create an environment which enables tumour development and growth. For example, they increase the expression of transforming growth factor-β and vascular endothelial growth factor, both of which are known to promote HCC tumourigenesis,. Several studies have shown that high CNI exposure is an independent risk factor for HCC recurrence and reduced recurrence-free survival. In these studies, high concentrations were defined as cyclosporin trough concentration of >300 ng/ml and tacrolimus trough concentration of >10 ng/ml. Further evidence of CNIs alone increasing HCC recurrence risk was shown in a large US retrospective cohort study with CNI monotherapy having a significantly increased risk compared with a combined CNI, antimetabolite and steroid immunosuppression regimen. Furthermore, cumulative dose exposure to cyclosporin has been shown to increase HCC recurrence post-transplant and reduce 5-year recurrence-free survival, particularly when these higher doses are administered in the 4–12 month interval post-transplantation. In contrast, these differences have only been observed in the first month with patients exposed to high-dose tacrolimus, with no significant difference noted after that,. The underlying reason for these differences between cyclosporin and tacrolimus is unclear and needs further assessment in larger prospective clinical trials.

sources.zraf034-s1/p3: Transplant benefit is defined as the gain offered by liver transplantation (LT) compared with the best alternative therapy (survival after LT minus survival with the best alternative treatment). The International Liver Transplantation Society (ILTS) Consensus guidelines on Transplant Oncology emphasized that transplant benefit should be one of the key parameters to be considered when defining optimal selection criteria for LT.
sources.zraf034-s2.1/p6: An increasing number of centres worldwide have started adopting LT for unresectable CRLM. Due to the scarcity of donor grafts in most countries and regions, many programmes have applied LDLT to be able to provide transplants to patients with CRLM, and the outcomes have largely been in line with other published results,. Systematic implementation of LDLT has, however, mostly been done in Asia, whereas the number of Western centres performing LDLT is limited. Split liver transplantation may offer a meaningful expansion of the donor pool, but the number of extra grafts obtained may be restricted by allocation policies in regions where MELD priority is used for prioritization on the waiting list. In 2015, the RAPID concept (Resection And Partial Liver Segment 2/3 Transplantation With Delayed Total Hepatectomy) was introduced as a possible method to provide liver transplantation for more patients with CRLM. The RAPID procedure entails an auxiliary segment 2 + 3 transplantation after a left hepatectomy. After reperfusion, the portal flow is diverted to the graft under portal pressure guidance to induce fast liver generation. Graft size is monitored weekly, and the second-stage hepatectomy can usually be performed 2–3 weeks post-transplant. A multicentre study among seven European centres has demonstrated that the RAPID procedure may be applied with adequate safety, good functional liver regeneration and second-stage hepatectomy after a median of 2 weeks. Moreover, RAPID can be applied both as a split liver technique in the deceased donor setting as well as with the use of living liver donors,. The latter is particularly attractive, since it possibly allows for a reduction in living donor risk whilst simultaneously offering a substantial treatment benefit for the CRLM recipient according to the double equipoise principle.
